title: Biographical Information; Family Background
description: Zoa Swayne provides details about her birth, her parents' origins, and her siblings. She then lists the names, birth dates, and occupations of her husband, Samuel, and their four sons.

title: Education; Teaching Career; Marriage Finances
description: She outlines her education at Albion Normal and the University of Idaho, and her work teaching grade school. She discusses the transition to being a housewife after marriage, the emotional difficulty of no longer earning her own income, and how the couple made joint financial decisions.

title: Hobbies; Community Organizations; Volunteer Work
description: She talks about her skills in cooking, sewing, and painting, and her extensive involvement in local groups. She mentions her work with the Clearwater Art Association, the Clearwater Historical Society, and the local museum, as well as her role illustrating a children's book.

title: Rural Living; Community Change; Depression Economy
description: She reflects on the benefits of rural life and how the town of Orfeo has grown and changed over the years. She recalls the financial hardships of the 1930s, including low wheat prices and the practice of teachers being paid in warrants.

title: Early Marriage; Financial Philosophy; Marital Roles
description: She recounts starting her married life in debt and her husband's early career. She contrasts modern installment buying with her own pay-as-you-go philosophy and explains her belief in marriage as an equal partnership where the wife provides subtle guidance.

title: Advice for Women; Parenting and Vocation
description: She offers advice on personal strength, goal setting, and community engagement. She describes how her sons chose their careers—law, veterinary medicine, and engineering—through aptitude testing and personal interest.

title: Child-rearing challenges; family planning
description: Zoa Swayne discusses the difficulties of raising children with large age gaps, noting that teenagers and preschoolers have conflicting needs. She expresses approval of modern family planning and young couples who set goals for having children.

title: Covered wagon journey west
description: Swayne recounts her family's 1919 migration from Washington State to southern Idaho in a covered wagon. She describes the wagon setup, crossing the Columbia River where a mare swam to follow her foal, the challenges of finding horse feed, and travel through Walla Walla and Boise.

title: Idaho homestead; mother's adjustment
description: Swayne describes arriving at their one-room homestead on the Camas Prairie, her mother's tears at the primitive conditions, and the harsh climate. She explains how her mother coped with the transition and notes that her father typically conducted exploratory trips before family moves.

title: Childhood recreation; farm labor
description: Swayne recalls childhood entertainments including baseball, Fourth of July picnics, and horse races. She describes working in the fields driving horses while her sister worked in the house, and driving a combine the summer before college when her father was injured.

title: Retirement activities; husband's work and hobbies
description: Leaving community activities behind, Swayne discusses her desire to focus on writing. She describes her husband's continued legal work, his tree-planting hobby and painting, and how their son John may take over the law practice.

title: Media and travel; caregiving for elderly mothers
description: Swayne lists favorite television programs and magazines including National Geographic. She discusses their travel history to Europe and Russia, explaining that they currently stay close to home to care for their elderly mothers.

title: Marriage roles; household finances; credit
description: After a brief interruption by a visitor (Isabel Miller), Swayne discusses how modern marriages require men to share housework rather than acting as 'lord of the manor.' She describes her financial arrangements, including income from a trailer that allows her independent spending, and their practice of avoiding long-term debt.
